680: You must fill the form before we speak. Then a second form, confirming we spoke.
681: There is a correct way to hand someone a document. I have practiced it for years.
682: You used blue ink. The form requires black. I am afraid we must begin again.
683: Protocol is not fussy. Protocol is care, expressed through the correct number of copies.
684: I do not make the rules. I merely know all of them, in order, from memory.
685: Before you may enter, please sign here, here, and, regrettably, also here.
686: A missing signature is a missing bridge between two nations. I take it seriously.
687: I arranged the chairs by rank. It took an hour. Nobody noticed. That means I did it right.
688: You may skip the small talk, but you may never skip the paperwork. Never.
689: Everything has a proper procedure. Even, I have found, the coffee break.
690: I keep three pens: one to sign, one to correct, and one for emergencies of protocol.
691: The form must be folded precisely so. A crooked fold is a small international incident.
692: I do not care what you say. I care very much where you sign it.
693: There is an order to these things, and the order is the whole point of these things.
694: A guest arrived without an appointment. I offered a form to request one. He left.
695: Protocol says I greet you before the tea. So: greetings. Now, your documents, please.
696: I have a stamp for approved, a stamp for pending, and a stamp I hope never to use.
697: Some people find the forms tedious. I find them calming. Each box has its place.
698: You may think this is only a formality. It is. And formalities are my life's work.
699: I filed your visit correctly. Whatever happens now, the paperwork will be immaculate.
700: I spoke for an hour at the reception. Afterward, no one could say what about. Perfect.
701: My calendar is dinners, dinners, and one more dinner. I have not cooked in years.
702: I can say that is a wonderful question in a way that means I will not answer it.
703: I gave a long speech about cooperation. Halfway through, even I stopped listening.
704: I have a smile for hello, a smile for goodbye, and a smile for when I cannot recall your name.
705: I nodded, I smiled, I agreed with everyone, and I promised absolutely nothing. A good day.
706: The secret to diplomacy is looking fascinated by a story you have heard forty times.
707: I attended the dinner, praised the soup at length, and quietly avoided every real topic.
708: People call me a great listener. Truly, I have simply learned to nod on time.
709: At every reception there is a buffet, and I am the only guest too busy talking to eat.
710: I can turn a simple yes into a graceful, hour-long maybe. It is a delicate art.
711: I have cut ribbons, planted trees, and unveiled plaques. I could not tell you what any of them marked.
712: I shook two hundred hands tonight. I recall none of them. I smiled at each one warmly.
713: When two sides disagree, I speak until they forget what they disagreed about.
714: I once agreed with two men who disagreed with each other. Both left pleased. That is the whole skill.
715: At dinners I sit through speeches in three languages and applaud all of them equally.
716: I raised my glass to peace, to friendship, and to whatever the occasion happened to be.
717: I have shaken hands on agreements I did not fully understand. The photographs came out lovely.
718: I can discuss the weather for a full hour and make it feel like statecraft.
719: I nod warmly through the interpreter, then again once I hear what was actually said.
